Assess structural quality only (subject length, a clear call to action, scannable body). This is advisory; be lenient and do not penalise legitimate creative variation.
Subject: Autumn trail tips for your next outing
CTA: Read more trail tips -> https://www.example.com/trail-tips/autumn
Body: Fall changes the trail in ways that matter.

Daylight shortens fast. In most of the northern Rockies and Appalachians, you lose roughly 2–3 minutes of usable light per day through October. If you're planning a 10-mile loop, run the math on your turnaround time before you leave the trailhead.

Leaf-fall hides trail markers, water bars, and roots. Pace down on descent. Wet leaves on packed dirt can approach the slip factor of wet rock — treat them accordingly.

Temperature swings widen. A 45°F morning can reach 65°F by noon and drop to 32°F after sunset at elevation. Layer for the low, not the high. Synthetics and wool move moisture when wet; cotton doesn't.

Water sources are inconsistent. Spring-fed streams often run stronger in fall, but surface water from summer rainfall is mostly gone. Check recent trip reports for your specific area, not just seasonal averages.

Navigation gets honest. Without foliage, you can often see terrain more clearly — use that. Take a bearing from a high point before you drop into a drainage. Fall is a good season to practice map and compass without relying on canopy gaps for GPS signal.

Mud and freeze cycles matter for footwear. If temps are swinging around freezing, waterproofing matters more than breathability for most day hikes. Know what your boots are and aren't built for before the trail tells you.

Have a good autumn out there.
